Artificial Intelligence.summary: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Detecting AI-Generated Videos with Spiking Neural Networks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Modern AI-generated videos are photorealistic at the single-frame level, leaving inter-frame dynamics as the main remaining axis for detection. Existing detectors typically handle this temporal evidence in three ways: feeding the full frame sequence to a generic temporal backbone, reducing one dominant temporal cue to fixed video-level descriptors, or comparing temporal features to real-video statistics through a detection metric. These strategies degrade sharply under cross-generator evaluation, where artifact type and timescale vary across generators. On caption-paired benchmark, GenVidBench, we identify two signatures that prior detectors do not jointly exploit: AI-generated videos exhibit smoother frame-to-frame temporal residuals at the pixel level, and more compact trajectories in the semantic feature space, indicating a temporal smoothness gap at both levels. We further observe that, when raw video is fed into a Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), fake clips elicit firing predominantly at object and motion boundaries, unlike real clips, suggesting that the SNN responds to temporal artifacts localized at edges. These cues are sparse, asynchronous, and concentrated at moments of change, which makes SNNs a natural choice for this task: their event-driven, sparsely-activated dynamics align with the structure of the residual signal in a way that dense ANN backbones do not. Building on this observation, we propose MAST, a detector that processes multi-channel temporal residuals with a spike-driven temporal branch alongside a frozen semantic encoder for cross-generator generalization. On the GenVideo benchmark, MAST achieves 93.14\% mean accuracy across 10 unseen generators under strict cross-generator evaluation, matching or surpassing the strongest ANN-based detectors and demonstrating the practical applicability of SNNs to AI-generated video detection.

Artificial Intelligence.title: AudioTurbo: Fast Text-to-Audio Generation with Rectified Diffusion
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Diffusion models have significantly improved the quality and diversity of text-to-audio (TTA) generation but are hindered by slow inference speed. Recent flow-based approaches have been explored for accelerating TTA generation. However, these approaches typically rely on dedicated flow-based generative frameworks and do not directly exploit existing pre-trained diffusion-based TTA models. To address this limitation while leveraging the strong generative capabilities of pre-trained diffusion models, we integrate rectified diffusion into these models to improve TTA generation efficiency. Specifically, we propose AudioTurbo, which learns first-order approximate ordinary differential equation (ODE) paths from deterministic noise-sample pairs generated by a pre-trained TTA model. Experiments show that our approach outperforms a flow-matching-based acceleration model in both generation quality and inference speed.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, 14 tables, including supplementary material

Artificial Intelligence.title: SPACE: Source-free Proxy Anchor Concept Erasure for MLLMs
Artificial Intelligence.summary: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face growing privacy risks and regulatory constraints, machine unlearning (MU) has emerged as a crucial solution for removing sensitive data while preserving model performance. However, existing MU methods typically rely on visual data of the target concepts, which is often unavailable due to strict data retention policies, thus creating a demand for source-free unlearning approaches that operate without access to the target data. In this work, we propose Source-free Proxy Anchor Concept Erasure (SPACE), the first source-free unlearning framework specialized for MLLMs. SPACE consists of two stages: (1) Text-Guided Proxy Anchor Selection (TPAS), which retrieves semantically aligned proxy anchors from the shared feature space. (2) Dual-Constraint Semantic Isolation (DCSI), which optimizes these anchors to indirectly erase target concepts. DCSI confines updates to the null space of retained knowledge, ensuring structural integrity. We theoretically prove that SPACE strictly bounds the perturbation on retained knowledge and maximizes feature spectral entropy, thereby maintaining the model's performance. Furthermore, extensive experiments across six datasets show that SPACE achieves performance comparable to that of state-of-the-art data-dependent methods, validating its effectiveness in source-free MU scenarios. The source code will be released.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 22 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. English translation of an article originally published in Bulgarian in Media and Language (2026). The original Bulgarian publication remains the version of record

Artificial Intelligence.title: Cautious Context Steering for Language Model Personalization
Artificial Intelligence.summary: User context can personalize a language model without per-user fine-tuning, but its influence is not equally helpful at every token. Context Steering (CoS) uses a fixed steering strength throughout generation and requires two LM forward passes per step. We propose Cautious Context Steering (CCS), a lightweight adapter that learns when and how strongly to steer a frozen LM using user context. We train the adapter through cautious distillation, using oracle targets built from predictions with and without context. It learns to match the steered distribution where context helps predict the user's preferred token and the context-free base distribution elsewhere. The CCS adapter outperforms both training-free context-based methods and trained personalization baselines in preference alignment across benchmarks. We also introduce GSM8K-P to evaluate task accuracy and task-specific format preferences together. CCS achieves high format adherence while maintaining task accuracy, offering a better balance than the baselines. The CCS adapter adds less than 0.4% of the backbone's parameters. At inference, each decoding step uses one context-conditioned LM forward pass and a lightweight adapter evaluation, reducing generation time on PRISM by approximately 35-36% compared with CoS.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Should a Voice Agent Speak? End-of-Turn Detection in Turkish
Artificial Intelligence.summary: A voice agent that waits for a fixed silence before replying either interrupts users who pause mid-utterance or responds late to users who have finished. This study examines the decision at the onset of silence, using turn ends and turn-internal pauses extracted from the Real-TurnTurk corpus of Turkish dyadic video calls. A fine-tuned Turkish TurnGPT model, a zero-shot Turkish language model and a deployed multilingual detector are compared, together with voice-activity timing and facial features, under recording-disjoint and speaker-disjoint evaluation with paired cluster bootstrap tests. On held-out recordings, the fine-tuned model separates turn ends from pauses better than both text baselines and is the best calibrated of the three. Timing features of the current speaker are similarly informative, and their combination with the fine-tuned text score gives the best timing-based results; with logistic regression, this combination also outperforms the same combination with either text baseline. In a latency simulation, adding the text score to a silence timeout shortens the mean response delay at the same interruption rate. On automatic Whisper transcripts, the fine-tuned model retains its advantage over the zero-shot model.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
Artificial Intelligence.summary: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $Θ(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $Σ_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.

Artificial Intelligence.title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at https://github.com/HeeSeung-Shin/Brats2026-Goat-HS.

Artificial Intelligence.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 26 pages, 11 figures, including appendix. Code: https://github.com/Gen-Verse/WeightCode

Artificial Intelligence.title: LLM-Based Threat Detection and Prevention Framework for IoT Ecosystems
Artificial Intelligence.summary: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced complex and evolving cybersecurity challenges. This paper presents a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for intelligent threat detection and prevention in IoT networks. The proposed architecture integrates two core components: a Detection Component that leverages fine-tuned models trained on IoT-specific datasets (IoT-23 and TON_IoT) to identify anomalous network behaviours, and a Prevention Component that generates adaptive response strategies to mitigate detected threats. The framework incorporates prompt management, local adaptation, and global refinement modules to support context-aware decision-making and continuous model-guided adaptation. Experimental validation in a Docker-based edge-cloud environment shows that BERT Small achieves 99.75% accuracy, F1-score, precision, and recall for threat detection, while the Prevention LLM achieves 98.3% accuracy in selecting suitable mitigation actions. These results highlight the potential of LLM-driven architectures to provide explainable and adaptive security solutions for next-generation IoT ecosystems.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: This paper has been accepted for publication at the IEEE GLOBECOM 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.

Artificial Intelligence.title: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: Visual Camouflage Attacks via HDR Gain Maps
Artificial Intelligence.summary: An image can pass automated safety checks while showing harmful content to its human viewer. We introduce DRJanus, a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between standard dynamic range (SDR) processing and high dynamic range (HDR) display. Automated systems often read only an image's SDR base, whereas HDR viewers reconstruct its appearance using an auxiliary gain map. DRJanus inverts this reconstruction to embed two independently chosen color images in a single JPEG, without querying or optimizing against the target model. It preserves the chosen SDR base exactly and reconstructs HDR targets at an average PSNR of 43.03 dB across 400 images. On a benchmark of 100 sexual-content images, DRJanus evades detection by all six tested commercial moderation services and nine vision-language models. Across five agents, each evaluated on 120 task cases per threat setting, attack success ranges from 31.67% to 100% for moderation evasion and from 95% to 100% for task manipulation. We also explore cross-view consistency checks as a mitigation. These findings expose a gap in visual trust: securing what a machine reads does not secure what a user sees. A demo is available at https://qshen0629.github.io/DRJanus/

Artificial Intelligence.title: Clause-Factored Bilateral State Grounding and Scoped Passivity for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Open-World Assumption (OWA) deduction requires distinguishing provable facts (True), refutations (False), and unprovable statements (Unknown) across counterfactual edits and unseen domains. Sequence and latent-recurrent transformers rely on distributional shortcuts, whereas chain-of-thought language models incur high autoregressive latency. We decompose OWA deduction into a clause-factored bilateral grounder ($F$) and a deductive deliberation operator ($B$), forming $B \circ F$ in Typed Edge-Factorized Bilateral Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation (TE-BPHD). Trained solely on three-way query labels without parsers or proof-depth annotations, TE-BPHD (37.85M parameters) maps clauses into a 1,440-dimensional Belnap space and propagates support through passivity-balanced implicit Port-Hamiltonian rule diodes. Across 17,036 locked ProofWriter test queries, TE-BPHD reaches 79.17 +/- 5.48% depth-5 counterfactual consistency (+23.83 to +38.67 percentage points over Seq2Seq T5, Flan-T5, and Recurrent-Depth T5) and 94.95 +/- 1.23% out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy across 5,270 six-domain queries (92.54 +/- 3.38% macro-mean). On a paired 120-query OOD slice, TE-BPHD attains 93.61 +/- 4.59% versus 79.17% for 3-shot Qwen3-1.7B under a 2,048-token reasoning cap (+14.44 percentage points) at 9.44 versus 14,878.4 ms/query batch-16 NVIDIA L4 throughput. Operator interventions show that symmetric single-rule passivity prevents positive two-cycle modes seen in Gain-Matched Unilateral Horn (+50.00 percentage points counterfactual consistency), whereas unit-interval Grounded Product-T-Norm Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) achieve cycle-safe OOD transfer (94.50 +/- 0.87%) without linear solves, and multi-fact ParaRules prose exposes an upstream grounding trade-off (1.33 +/- 1.76% zero-shot vs. 34.11 +/- 5.01% with five-slot optimal-transport joint grounding).
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 17 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Revised manuscript with expanded 17,036-query ProofWriter evaluation, 3-shot Qwen3-1.7B CoT comparison, Grounded Product-T-Norm LTN operator intervention, and updated Figure 2

Artificial Intelligence.title: Demonstration-Free Skill Composition for Navigation and Manipulation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 10 pages. Accepted at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026). Project page: https://madeleinenouri.github.io/acra-skill-composition

Artificial Intelligence.title: LoongForge-Embodied: A Unified Framework for Training Heterogeneous Embodied Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Raptor: Rejection-aware Adaptive Tree based on Speculative Decoding
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Think Once, Act Fast: Cost-Effective Recursive Self-Improvement for Decision Model Harness
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Paint-Anything: Unified Any-Color Control for Image Generation and Editing
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Professional design requires any-color control: the ability to specify an object's target color with any 24-bit hex value for image generation and editing. Prior work has explored color generation, editing, and colorization, but often relies on dedicated color representations or specialized inference procedures. Advances in large language models offer a simpler starting point: even compact models can associate hex values with color semantics. We present Paint-Anything, which learns a shared hex-prompt interface for generation and editing through object-level color supervision. We develop a data pipeline that constructs Paint-500K from real images through object grounding, perceptual color labeling, and editing-pair synthesis. Since shadows make real-image labels only approximate colors, we complement this supervision with pure-color anchors whose pixels exactly match their paired hex values. These anchors are used only at high-noise timesteps, leaving low-noise training to natural images. We further introduce Any Color Benchmark (ACBench), comprising ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit, to measure object-level hex color fidelity across both tasks. On FLUX.2-4B, Paint-Anything improves ACBench-T2I and ACBench-Edit scores by 85.3% and 28.3%, respectively, relative to the base model, with ablations supporting the training recipe. It also achieves the highest average CompColor score among the compared methods.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 31 pages, Seed Technical Report

Artificial Intelligence.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain.
  We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses.
  We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of 30 real-world PHP applications identifies 20 vulnerabilities and 13 exploit chains, nine of which achieve remote code execution (RCE).

Computation and Language.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
Computation and Language.summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

Computation and Language.title: Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

Computation and Language.title: Capturing In-Context Learning Dynamics with Task Operators
Computation and Language.summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to perform new tasks from demonstrations without weight updates. However, every ICL inference requires processing the full set of examples, resulting in inefficient deployments, and how ICL works mechanistically is not fully understood. Prior work compresses ICL into fixed activation vectors extracted from specific layers or positions, but these input-independent interventions fail on complex tasks where the output depends on fine-grained interactions with the input. By analyzing the ICL forward pass, we show that each attention head's output is an affine transformation of its context-masked counterpart, and that the parameters of this transformation are empirically stable across samples for a given task. Building on this, we introduce Task Operator (TO), which replays this transformation as an analytically derived update to the attention output projection. Across lexical, algorithmic, and reasoning tasks, TO achieves the best overall performance among prior methods and substantially narrows the gap between zero-shot inference and ICL. We further show that the extracted knowledge concentrates in a task-specific sparse circuit across layers and positions, and that averaging operators from disjoint demonstration batches enables effective many-shot scaling without expanding the context window. Our code is available at https://github.com/gzxiong/task_operator.

Computation and Language.title: Rethinking Visual Attribution for Chest X-ray Reasoning in Large Vision Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) show promise in medical applications, but their inability to faithfully ground responses in visual evidence raises serious concerns about clinical trustworthiness. While visual attribution methods are widely used to explain LVLM predictions, whether these explanations actually reflect the visual evidence underlying the model's decision is largely unverified, since ground-truth annotations for internal model reasoning are typically unavailable. We address this question for chest X-ray (CXR) reasoning by developing a causal evaluation framework that retains only CXR-VQA samples for which the expert-annotated region is verified, via counterfactual editing, to be causally responsible for the model's prediction. Using this framework across 11 attribution methods, six open-source LVLMs, and two output modes (direct answer and step-by-step reasoning), we find that existing attribution methods often fail to identify the evidence used by LVLMs. To address this failure, we propose MedFocus, a concept-based attribution method that localizes clinically meaningful anatomical regions via unbalanced optimal transport and measures their causal effect on model outputs through targeted interventions. MedFocus produces spatial, concept-level, and token-level attributions and substantially outperforms prior methods, taking a step toward more trustworthy attribution for medical LVLMs. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/gzxiong/medfocus/.

Computation and Language.title: Don't Lose Focus: Activation Steering via Key-Orthogonal Projections
Computation and Language.summary: Activation steering controls LLM behaviour towards target behaviour by intervening in internal representations, yet it often degrades reasoning and retrieval performance. We argue that a primary cause of this trade-off is attention rerouting: steering vectors alter query-key matching, shifting attention away from contextually important tokens toward less informative ones. To address this, we propose Steering via Key-Orthogonal Projections (SKOP), a steering method that constrains harmful attention rerouting without eliminating steering efficacy. SKOP achieves this by preserving attention patterns on a small set of focus tokens the model relies on for reasoning and retrieval, while allowing redistribution among less critical tail tokens. Across multiple steering benchmarks, we show that SKOP achieves the best joint steering-utility trade-off, reducing utility degradation by 5-7x while retaining over 95% of vanilla steering efficacy. Our results further suggest that, in long-context retrieval settings where vanilla steering approaches are ineffective, SKOP can maintain robust performance by avoiding attention rerouting.

Computation and Language.title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
Computation and Language.summary: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($Δd' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.

Computation and Language.title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to perform a form of conditional inference. In-context learning is one implicit way to do this. The prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Translating these comparisons into a benchmark score and evaluating frontier models across problem domains, we demonstrate widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting further reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. The effect persists across variations in partitioning, verbalization, and estimation task, suggesting that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.

Computation and Language.title: Natural Language Processing: An Applied Research Practicum From Classical Text Processing to Multimodal and Agentic Systems
Computation and Language.summary:
This preprint presents a systematic, research-oriented guide to modern natural language processing, covering the full NLP pipeline from tokenisation, text normalisation, vector representations, and classical machine learning to transformer architectures, large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, preference-based alignment, and multimodal systems.
  The material comprises eighteen practical works combining theoretical foundations, reproducible implementation examples, detailed experimental procedures, evaluation metrics, and research-oriented assignments. Each work includes three structured core tasks and optional advanced investigations. Common requirements for reporting, data provenance, experimental evaluation, and reproducibility are established across the guide.
  Particular attention is devoted to low-resource and morphologically rich languages, including Tajik, Tatar, and Bashkir. The guide addresses subword tokenisation, cross-lingual transfer, machine translation, language model adaptation, and the evaluation of NLP systems under limited data and computational resources.
  Advanced topics include prompt engineering, reasoning strategies, multi-agent collaboration, model compression, efficient inference, AI safety, and LLMOps. A capstone project integrates methods from different chapters into the development and evaluation of domain-specific NLP systems.
  The guide is intended for senior undergraduate students, graduate students, researchers, and developers interested in implementing and critically evaluating NLP methods.
Computation and Language.comment: 146 pages, 18 practical works, a capstone project, and accompanying Python examples. Substantially expanded core tasks, reorganized material, and updated bibliography. Major revision of the previous version

Computation and Language.title: LipSpell: A Language-Independent Phonetic Scoring Framework for Spelling Correction Combining Distinctive-Feature Edit Distance, Keyboard Geometry, and Corpus Frequency
Computation and Language.summary: Automatic spelling correction must handle both keyboard typographical slips and cognitive or phonetic misspellings where writers approximate a word's pronunciation. Conventional spell checkers rely either on orthographic edit distance and keyboard proximity--which struggle when phonetic errors diverge by multiple characters--or on English-centric phonetic hashes such as Soundex and Metaphone. We present LipSpell, a unified, language-independent phonetic scoring engine paired with swappable language-specific G2P frontends, keyboard maps, and lexicons integrating: (1) a precomputed |P|x|P| phone-distance matrix from universal IPA distinctive features, (2) physical keyboard geometry, and (3) corpus unigram frequency priors, accelerated by a two-stage symmetric-delete and seven-class phonetic-code index. Across six English benchmarks (including 1,000 L2 errors from TOEFL-Spell), LipSpell outperforms Norvig and Hunspell on every dataset and beats Aspell on Norvig1 (78.52% vs. 75.56%), Holbrook (32.00% vs. 26.67%), and TOEFL-Spell (77.30% vs. 72.80%). Evaluated across six languages spanning five branches (Germanic, Romance, Slavic, Semitic, Turkic), three families (Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic, Turkic), and three scripts, LipSpell achieves strong fixed-weight transfer on Brazilian Portuguese (73.00% Top-1 on n=500 Wikipedia without NFD tolerance and 75.80% with NFD vs. 66.40% Norvig, 64.20% Hunspell, 64.00% Aspell) and Russian Cyrillic (85.67% vs. 78.50% Norvig). On 50/50 clean non-word splits with lexicon cleaning and weak-character indels, tuning yields strong gains over Norvig in Portuguese (86.97% vs. 76.75%), Turkish (81.67% vs. 79.05%), Hebrew Abjad (74.59% vs. 62.30%), and French (74.53% vs. 67.92%), while fixed weights remain optimal for English (80.37%) and Russian (85.67%).

Computation and Language.title: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents
Computation and Language.summary: Real applications provide the training setting closest to phone-agent deployment, but are difficult to reset, scale safely, and verify programmatically. Static screenshots and interaction trajectories preserve realistic evidence but cannot generate new experience. We introduce PhoneWorld, a trace-grounded framework that converts such evidence into runnable, resettable, and verifiable Android environments. PhoneWorld induces a usage-weighted interaction skeleton from observed pages, transitions, and state-changing operations; translates it into a behavior-grounded app specification; realizes the specification through an autonomous build--inspect--repair loop; and synthesizes executable tasks with programmatic verifiers. The resulting suite spans 34 consumer-facing apps across 16 domains and supports an audited online benchmark, verified trajectory generation, and online RL through common reset and verification interfaces. Evaluations with diverse general and open-source GUI agents show that PhoneWorld supports reliable end-to-end online interaction and exposes capabilities complementary to AndroidWorld. Controlled SFT experiments further show that PhoneWorld trajectories complement AndroidWorld supervision, transfer across online and offline benchmarks, and become more effective as data volume and app coverage increase. Under a matched RL budget, combining PhoneWorld mock-app rollouts with real-app rollouts improves performance over real-app RL alone on both real-phone tasks and AndroidWorld. Together, these results demonstrate that trace-grounded executable abstraction can bridge realistic mobile behavior and scalable agent learning, turning limited real-app evidence into a growing supply of controllable and verifiable environments for training and evaluation.

Computation and Language.title: MINTEval: Evaluating Memory under Multi-Target Interference in Long-Horizon Agent Systems
Computation and Language.summary: Real-world agents operate over long and evolving horizons, where information is repeatedly updated and may interfere across memories, requiring accurate recall and aggregated reasoning over multiple pieces of information. However, existing benchmarks focus on static, independent recall and fail to capture these dynamic interactions between evolving memories. In this paper, we study how current memory-augmented agents perform in realistic, interference-heavy, long-horizon settings across diverse domains and question types. We introduce MINTEval (Long-Horizon Memory under INTerference Evaluation), a benchmark featuring (1) long, highly interconnected contexts with frequently updated information that induces substantial interference, (2) diverse domains (state tracking, multi-turn dialogue, Wikipedia revisions, and GitHub commits), enabling evaluation of domain generalization, and (3) diverse question types that assess robustness to interference, including (i) single-target recall tasks requiring retrieval of a specific target from long contexts, and (ii) multi-target aggregation tasks requiring reasoning over multiple relevant pieces of information. Overall, MINTEval has 15.6k question-answering pairs over long-horizon contexts averaging 138.8k tokens and extending up to 1.8M tokens per instance. We evaluate 7 representative systems, including vanilla long-context LLMs, RAG, and memory-augmented agent frameworks. Across all systems, we observe consistently low performance (avg. 27.9% accuracy), especially on questions requiring aggregated reasoning over multiple pieces of evidence. Our analysis shows that performance is primarily limited by retrieval and memory construction. Furthermore, current memory systems struggle to recall and reason over earlier facts that are revised or interfered with by subsequent context, with accuracy degrading as the number of intervening updates increases.
Computation and Language.comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Camera-Ready); Equal contribution; order decided by a coin flip. Code and data: https://github.com/amy-hyunji/MINTEval

Computation and Language.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Government Scheme Search in English and Marathi
Computation and Language.summary: Retrieving government schemes requires matching citizens' information needs to formal administrative descriptions, often across languages and terminology. We present a bilingual search system for Maharashtra government schemes and public services that combines BM25 retrieval with sentence-embedding similarity through equal-weight score fusion. The system indexes aligned English-Marathi scheme descriptions and supports multilingual, Marathi-focused, and translation-mediated semantic configurations. Evaluation on manually curated bilingual queries compares BM25, dense retrieval, and hybrid retrieval using IndicSBERT and MahaSBERT. BM25 provides a strong baseline with a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.864. Hybrid retrieval increases MRR to 0.872 with IndicSBERT and 0.879 with MahaSBERT, whereas the corresponding dense-only systems achieve 0.663 and 0.655. MahaSBERT-based fusion also increases precision from 0.781 to 0.808 while matching BM25 recall at 0.946. These results support the complementary use of lexical and semantic signals in this collection, while showing that improvements over a strong lexical baseline are modest and metric-dependent. The study provides an application-focused analysis of hybrid retrieval for bilingual public-service information access.

Computation and Language.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
Computation and Language.summary: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

Computation and Language.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
Computation and Language.summary:
Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters.
  Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens.
  Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.

Computation and Language.title: Multimodal Error Detection in Chest X-ray Reports: A Large Language Model Reading Image Evidence
Computation and Language.summary: Rad-Linter checks chest X-ray reports against image-derived evidence to flag potential errors for review. A pretrained image classifier supplies scores for nine pathologies, and a 1.5B-parameter language model, fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,816 examples, checks their consistency with the report. We compare it with a keyword-and-negation rule baseline given the same reports and scores. Evaluation uses controlled report-score pairings from OpenI, with consistency labels derived from automatic report labels and score thresholds. Each counterfactual quad crosses two real reports with two real score vectors from other patients, creating two consistent and two inconsistent pairs. Every report and score vector occurs in both conditions, so either input alone permits only 50% accuracy. On 131 quads, Rad-Linter achieves 98.5% pair accuracy versus 80.5% for the rule baseline, and classifies all four pairs correctly in 94.4% of quads versus 56.5%. The checkers perform similarly on omission items, including unmentioned and negated findings; larger differences occur on the remaining item types, which require interpreting how findings are described. The same language model without fine-tuning remains near 50% accuracy. On a second set of 181 quads that also includes reports on which the automatic labelers disagree, pair accuracy is 93.4% versus 75.3%. These controlled results show that, given the same image-derived scores, a trained language model detects report-score inconsistencies more accurately than the tested rule baseline, with the advantage concentrated in interpreting how findings are worded.

Computation and Language.title: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization
Computation and Language.summary: Linear attention replaces growing KV caches with fixed-size recurrent states, yet these persistent states can become a substantial memory bottleneck under concurrent serving. Directly quantizing recurrent states to low precision often leads to severe accuracy degradation, as quantization errors propagate through successive state updates. We discover that the impact of these errors depends on two complementary dimensions: temporally, errors in long-lived memory can persist across many decoding steps; spatially, errors in different key rows affect model outputs differently, while state magnitudes vary substantially along both rows and columns. Motivated by these observations, we propose STEPQuant, a spatial-temporal post-training quantization framework for Delta-rule recurrent states. STEPQuant allocates precision according to error magnitude and memory lifetime, and jointly fits key-row and value-column scales based on state distributions and key-row impact on output error. Experiments on Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct across both long- and short-generation benchmarks show that STEPQuant closely matches FP32-state accuracy under a nominal 6-bit budget and outperforms uniform INT8 in its 4-bit configuration. Integrated into SGLang with optimized GPU kernels, 6-bit STEPQuant achieves over 5x recurrent-state compression and reduces total serving memory by up to 68.7%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dreamer-Toby/STEPQuant.
Computation and Language.comment: Technical report; v2: Expanded experiments and evaluations

Computation and Language.title: LongBEL: Long-Context and Document-Consistent Biomedical Entity Linking
Computation and Language.summary: Biomedical entity linking maps textual mentions to concepts in structured knowledge bases such as UMLS or SNOMED CT. Most existing systems link each mention independently, using only the mention or its surrounding sentence. This ignores dependencies between mentions in the same document and can lead to inconsistent predictions, especially when the same concept appears under different surface forms. We introduce LongBEL, a document-level generative framework that combines full-document context with a memory of previous predictions. To make this memory robust, LongBEL is trained with cross-validated predictions rather than gold labels, reducing the mismatch between training and inference and limiting cascading errors. Experiments on five biomedical benchmarks across English, French, and Spanish show that LongBEL improves over sentence-level generative baselines, with the largest gains on datasets where concepts frequently recur within documents. An ensemble of local, global, and memory-based variants achieves the best results across all benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the largest gains occur on recurring concepts, suggesting that LongBEL mainly improves document-level consistency rather than isolated mention disambiguation.

Computation and Language.title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
Computation and Language.summary: Empirical legal scholarship increasingly treats judicial text as data, and much of it still runs on sparse, interpretable pipelines -- TF-IDF features and linear classifiers -- because the textual feature is often the object of study rather than a means to prediction. Yet these pipelines inherit preprocessing defaults from mid-century information retrieval that were never validated against classification accuracy. The most entrenched of these is stopword removal. This study introduces an exhaustive single word ablation that measures the effect of a preprocessing step directly against the downstream objective, and applies it to stopword removal as the hardest case to dislodge. Matching Supreme Court Database labels to Caselaw Access Project opinion texts, the study examines two binary tasks that bracket F1 headroom, ideological direction (no-removal baseline F1 ~0.68) and constitutional versus non-constitutional law type (~0.92), across 7,668 and 7,001 opinions. For each task, the ablation removes each of about 18,500 candidate words in turn, and a task-specific stoplist is built from the measurements. Common generic stoplists fall below the no-removal baseline in all twelve held-out tests. The task-specific stoplists move held-out F1 by +0.0023 (95% CI [-0.0124, +0.0170]) on ideology and by +0.0001 ([-0.0082, +0.0085]) on law type. Neither task shows a detectable benefit from removal, and supplemental analysis finds that word-level statistics predict removal effects poorly, because true removal effects differ by less than the measurement can register, leaving little to predict. The method generalizes to any inherited preprocessing default; the result is a caution specific to interpretable legal text-as-data, where a step that reshapes which features a model sees can distort the doctrinal and ideological signal the research is meant to recover. The burden of proof sits with removal.

Computation and Language.title: MemFolder: Structure-Guided Memory Folding for Efficient Agent Memory Management
Computation and Language.summary: Long-term agents accumulate large external memory stores as interactions unfold, increasing the costs of storage, retrieval, and response generation. Efficiency is constrained by two coupled factors: a growing record count increases retrieval overhead, while longer retrieved contexts increase prefill computation and decoding-time attention costs. Existing methods prune or consolidate records, but pruning can discard useful evidence, whereas consolidation may produce fewer yet longer retrieval units. We introduce MemFolder, a structure-guided memory folding framework that sequentially reduces record count and context length. The framework comprises two core components that share memory groups, using cross-record structure to guide both evidence consolidation and compact representation. RecordFolder grounds entity mentions, progressively selects representative yet complementary anchors, and combines semantic and entity affinity with temporal chaining to consolidate compatible records into fewer retrieval units. ContextFolder encodes the original records within these groups into compact text and uses verification feedback to revise encodings when key facts cannot be recovered. Experiments on the three text-based memory benchmarks LoCoMo, PersonaMem, and LongMemEval and the two multimodal benchmarks M3-Bench-web and M3-Bench-robot demonstrate the strong performance of our methods. Notably, on Mem0, RecordFolder retains 99.0% of the original average performance across the three text-based benchmarks with 50% fewer records, exceeding the strongest baseline by 1.9 percentage points in performance retention. Combined with ContextFolder, existing record compression methods further shorten their output records while retaining most of their performance.

Computation and Language.title: Balance of Benchmarks: Evidence Retention and Multiplicity-Aware Model Comparison
Computation and Language.summary: Benchmark aggregation requires decisions about how much evidence to use and how much influence each benchmark receives. Curated suites control influence through selection, which can exclude informative observations. A broader pool can retain those observations. With equal weighting, repeated or closely related benchmarks gain influence as their number grows. We introduce Balance of Benchmarks (BoB) to retain eligible observations and control their influence separately. We fit benchmark-specific response curves to place different difficulty ranges on a shared ability scale and use description similarity to downweight benchmarks in crowded neighborhoods. We test retention and density weighting in separate interventions on WildScores, a sparse collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks, using 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks as a controlled reference. With the model population fixed and entire source-lineage families held out, suite expansion improves held-out prediction under BoB and equal-weight equating on both WildScores and BIG-bench. Under substantial reporting overlap, density weighting improves robustness to multiplicity. Complete re-listings yield smaller mean rank displacement under BoB (0.63 versus 1.95 for equal-weight equating), with benefits also in paraphrased re-listings and supported affine fits. The benefit can reverse if models report different benchmarks, because a single weight per column gives models that report only part of a group less than its intended share. We therefore compute each model's weights from the benchmarks it reports. This rule removes the reversal in controlled re-listings and keeps held-out prediction close to that of equal weighting. These comparisons separate evidence retention, benchmark influence, and reporting coverage and show why repeated entries need to be handled per model.
Computation and Language.comment: 40 pages. Revised analysis of evidence retention and per-model weighting. Includes appendix details and WildScores data

Computation and Language.title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
Computation and Language.summary: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.
Computation and Language.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at WDSA/CCWI 2026. Proceedings publication pending
