However, as standard datasets in this space often cover small classes of physical behavior, it can be difficult to evaluate the efficacy of new approaches. To address this gap, we introduce the Well: a large-scale collection of datasets containing numerical simulations of a wide variety of spatiotemporal physical systems. The Well draws from domain experts and numerical software developers to provide 15TB of data across 16 datasets covering diverse domains such as biological systems, fluid dynamics, acoustic scattering, as well as magneto-hydrodynamic simulations of extra-galactic fluids or supernova explosions. These datasets can be used individually or as part of a broader benchmark suite. To facilitate usage of the Well, we provide a unified PyTorch interface for training and evaluating models. We demonstrate the function of this library by introducing example baselines that highlight the new challenges posed by the complex dynamics of the Well. The code and data is available at https://github.com/PolymathicAI/the_well.
Machine Learning.comment: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks

Machine Learning.title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
Machine Learning.summary: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.

Machine Learning.title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

Machine Learning.title: Highly Efficient Vertical Federated Clustering with Triangle-Inequality-based Pruning
Machine Learning.summary: In many real-world scenarios, multiple parties hold complementary feature subsets for the same samples but cannot share raw data. This makes efficient clustering over distributed feature subsets an important and challenging problem. While vertical federated learning (VFL) enables such collaboration, existing VFL clustering methods often require many communication rounds or substantial local computation. To address these limitations, we first propose TriCD, an exact pruning method for CDKM that preserves the same cluster assignments under the same initialization. TriCD constructs triangle-inequality bounds on demand to skip redundant objective evaluations with negligible extra space. Building upon this, we propose FedTriCD, an efficient federated clustering algorithm. By decomposing the global objective into client-local subproblems, FedTriCD enables pruning-based local optimization using only local data. FedTriCD further reduces communication by allowing multiple local updates between server synchronizations. A proximal regularization term is introduced to control the drift caused by infrequent communication. Our theoretical analysis establishes the exactness and finite convergence of TriCD and provides a bounded-error server-side update guarantee for FedTriCD. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the efficiency and clustering quality of the proposed methods. TriCD achieves up to a 50.07$\times$ speedup over \Lloyd's algorithm. Moreover, FedTriCD achieves competitive clustering quality while requiring fewer local evaluations and fewer communication rounds than state-of-the-art federated clustering methods.

Machine Learning.title: Federated and Balanced $k$-means: Communication Efficiency, Privacy, and Heterogeneity
Machine Learning.summary: Collaborating on data across organizations in healthcare and finance demands methods that preserve privacy while enabling effective analysis. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates clustering across data where different parties hold different features of the same entities without sharing raw data. However, existing VFL clustering methods suffer from two key limitations: vulnerability to information leakage and the creation of imbalanced clusters. To address these limitations, we propose Fabric, a balanced and privacy-preserving federated $k$-means algorithm. Our method decomposes the balanced clustering problem into independent subproblems for each client, using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently handle the balance constraints. Under the semi-honest model, Fabric provides provable privacy guarantees by injecting calibrated noise into local objective evaluations. Extensive evaluations on ten real-world datasets show that Fabric achieves a superior utility-privacy trade-off compared with state-of-the-art methods and converges faster. Specifically, Fabric reduces SSE by 29.1\% on average and improves balance performance by 1.41$\times$, while being 26$\times$ faster on average.

Machine Learning.title: Geometry-Preserving Neural Architectures on Manifolds with Boundary
Machine Learning.summary: A growing number of neural architectures have been developed to enforce geometric constraints, including projection-based networks, exponential-map updates, and manifold neural ODEs. In this paper, we study several such architectures, with the goal of understanding their approximation-theoretic properties and trade-offs. We distinguish between architectures that enforce constraints at intermediate layers and those that enforce constraints only at the output. For projected neural ODEs on uniformly prox-regular sets, we establish stability estimates and derive universal approximation results on compact smooth manifolds, including manifolds with boundary. In particular, we establish universal approximation of measurable manifold-valued maps in the $L^2$ topology. In contrast, architectures that enforce constraints only at the output can admit uniform approximation guarantees for continuous target maps under suitable geometric assumptions. We further investigate how the choice of constraint-enforcing map, namely metric projection or the Riemannian exponential map, affects these guarantees. While both constructions can be used to preserve constraints at intermediate layers, their use at the output leads to different approximation properties. In particular, exponential-map output architectures can encounter topological obstructions to uniform approximation, motivating approximation guarantees in $L^2$. On the other hand, metric projection-based output architectures can retain uniform approximation guarantees when the constraint set has positive reach. Our study raises the broader question of when the additional complexity of enforcing constraints at intermediate layers, as motivated by neural ODE approaches, and different choices of constraint-enforcing map are justified by the resulting benefits in approximation and learning performance.

Machine Learning.title: When Scores Conflict with Preferences: Pre-Alignment Diagnosis and Adaptive Correction of Constraint Drift in DPO
Machine Learning.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is increasingly used in settings where pairwise preferences coexist with pointwise criteria such as response length, answer correctness, or safety scores. When the two disagree, standard DPO treats pairs whose preferred output scores worse on the pointwise criterion (conflict pairs) in the same way as the remaining (matching) pairs. We characterize a systematic failure mode, constraint drift: for sufficiently small updates, conflict pairs tend to increase constraint cost while matching pairs tend to repair it, and the net change depends on their balance. This balance yields a closed-form pre-alignment diagnostic, $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$, computable from dataset statistics, that indicates whether a dataset is self-correcting or requires intervention. Building on this diagnostic, we propose Conflict-aware DPO (CoDPO), which down-weights conflict pairs with a strength set from $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ rather than tuned, and adds an adaptive margin shift that addresses residual drift during training. Empirically, drift grows monotonically with conflict exposure on the conflict-dominated domains, and the intervention decision given by $ρ^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ matches the observed drift on every domain, including one that it identifies as self-correcting. On all four domains of the main comparison, CoDPO reduces drift while largely preserving the preference learning of vanilla DPO. Compared with hard filtering and recent constrained and multi-objective baselines, CoDPO also achieves a more favorable drift-preference trade-off.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Corresponding author: Yan Yan

Machine Learning.title: A Two-Parameter Weibull Framework for Diagnosing Transformer Weight Distributions
Machine Learning.summary:
Transformer checkpoints contain billions of weights, yet how their element-wise distributions vary across components, models, and training is hard to characterize. We fit the magnitude distribution of each analyzed weight matrix with a two-parameter Weibull reference model under a fixed middle-80% protocol. For i.i.d. Gaussian initialization, the corresponding half-Normal target has protocol-fitted shape $k_0 \approx 1.20$. Matched comparisons with gamma and lognormal favor Weibull for most component groups; support is less decisive for separately stored MHA query/key projections, and no tested single family cleanly describes matrices carrying a secondary weight population.
  Across 12 model entries spanning seven families, terminal FFN shape medians fall in a narrow band, $k \in [1.186, 1.204]$ (CV $= 0.51\%$), whereas query/key projections show architecture-associated departures. This stability is macroscopic only: in the five Pythia models whose released step-0 checkpoints permit a paired comparison, FFN and attention-output matrices remain near the reference shape despite large displacement and reorientation, so terminal shape similarity is not explained by parameter proximity alone. The fitted shape $k$ is read as a reference-relative central-body shape indicator and the scale $λ$ as a magnitude coordinate; neither is presented as a predictor of downstream performance. In a Qwen case study, the screen localizes a shallow-FFN secondary small-magnitude population, and direct raw-weight analysis of a flagged block traces much of that population to coherently suppressed intermediate channels. The method requires only released checkpoints and complements behavioral and structural analyses. The code and reference database are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.
Machine Learning.comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. 40 pages. Updated to the final accepted version, including practical-use guidance. Journal version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=j7qGffCwDa

Machine Learning.title: Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure
Machine Learning.summary: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.

Machine Learning.title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

Machine Learning.title: Reliable Behavior Discovery via False Discovery Rate Control
Machine Learning.summary: Reliable methods for discovering behavior patterns in large generative models are increasingly essential as models become both more complex and capable. We formalize behavior discovery as a problem class of interest and highlight the task of controlling false discovery rate (FDR) as crucial for guaranteeing reliability in behavior discovery. Building upon the multiple hypothesis testing literature, we propose DISCO (Discovery through Iterative Search with COarsened $e$-processes), a method which provably controls FDR in behavior discovery under mild conditions. DISCO improves power over previous related eBH-based approaches by allowing for adaptivity to a data-dependent number of hypotheses to be tested. We demonstrate empirically that DISCO controls FDR with higher power than comparable approaches on both synthetic data and a novel empirical evaluation of FDR-controlling methods in settings where large generative models act as both discovery engines and targets. Code is available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/disco .

Machine Learning.title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
Machine Learning.summary: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions.

Machine Learning.title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
Machine Learning.summary: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code, dataset, and benchmark leaderboard available at https://egosurghands.github.io

Machine Learning.title: Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency
Machine Learning.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. Specifically, we represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two complementary axes: dependence explained by semantic support versus additional reasoning history, and dependence allocated to answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning. This decomposition yields global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency. Controlled interventions show that the proposed metrics respond to hidden dependence and induced off-path reasoning as intended. Across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks, answer-level unfaithfulness is consistently associated with greater predictive uncertainty, whereas both unfaithfulness and inefficiency exhibit weak or inconsistent associations with answer correctness. We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.

Machine Learning.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
Machine Learning.summary: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.

Machine Learning.title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
Machine Learning.summary: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.

Machine Learning.title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz
Machine Learning.summary: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with latent states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the ordinary ranges, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On the 64 deterministic systems, the two strongest agents solve 39 and 31, and classical and neural baselines together 14. The difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in the data: in 55% of the agents' failed investigations, the experiments they bought suffice once the true program is given with unknown coefficients. We also start agents on a related system from the program of a first system, either the one they discovered or the true one; agents holding a correct program solve the related system in 15 of 42 investigations, and agents without one in 5 of 64. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents that find a system's variables still miss how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to ones that predict better.

Machine Learning.title: ORION: Exact Canonical-State Supervision for Systematic Generalization in Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: Autoregressive Transformers generally fail on out-of-distribution reasoning due to two primary reasons: positional corruption over long sequences and structural state drift across deep execution steps. We introduce ORION, a framework that supervises exact canonical execution states via auxiliary heads to anchor latent trajectories to valid computational manifolds. Across Folding, GridShift, and CLRS-30, a pre-registered 2 x 2 factorial shows that RoPE and ORION address orthogonal axes. RoPE recovers length extrapolation (59.8%), while ORION recovers depth extrapolation (66.7%). Moreover, their combination complementarily achieves strict additive gain in joint length-depth extrapolation, while either method alone offers near satisfactory results. Negative controls confirm that the gain depends strictly on exact canonical alignment; hashed state statistics fail to constrain depth extrapolation.

Machine Learning.title: Auditing and Adapting kNNGuard for Long-Context Prompts
Machine Learning.summary: Training-free activation guardrails such as kNNGuard score prompts by comparing last-token LLM hidden states (the Layer Ensemble branch, kNNGuard LE) and sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Embedding-kNN) against a small reference bank (50 examples per class), combining the two branches into a Fused Ensemble (kNNGuard FE). While effective on short inputs (up to 256 tokens), standard kNNGuard degrades substantially on long inputs (over 1000 tokens): averaged across Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-E4B-it, kNNGuard LE AUROC drops from 0.742 (0.777 and 0.706) to 0.554 (0.587 and 0.521) on Content Harm Moderation (Aegis-2.0), and from 0.994 (0.995 and 0.992) to 0.556 (0.598 and 0.513) on RAG Hallucination Detection (HaluBench). We trace this degradation to three causes: (1) hidden-state drift as sequence length increases, (2) hard 256-token truncation in MiniLM, and (3) signal dilution when a long document is compressed into a single final-token vector. We then evaluate three training-free adaptations: a Length-Routed Dual Bank, a long-context embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), and Strided Window Pooling across intermediate token positions. On Content Harm Moderation, dual-bank routing and strided window pooling raise long-context kNNGuard LE AUROC from 0.554 to 0.828 (+0.274 AUROC) and fused kNNGuard FE AUROC from 0.721 to 0.886 (+0.164 AUROC) with no latency overhead from bank routing. On RAG Hallucination Detection, where the guardrail must verify logical consistency between a generated answer and a retrieved passage, sentence-embedding kNN remains near random chance across all lengths, while length-matched LLM hidden states (kNNGuard LE) recover medium-length detection (AUROC = 0.853) but remain limited on over-1000-token passages (AUROC = 0.607) due to final-token dilution over long contexts.

Machine Learning.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
Machine Learning.summary: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

Machine Learning.title: Accelerating Muon with Spectral Residual Correction
Machine Learning.summary: Muon constructs matrix updates by applying a matrix-sign transformation to momentum. A common route to accelerating Muon is to modify the gradient or momentum before this transformation. We explore a complementary direction: refining the parameter step while retaining Muon's momentum recursion. Derived from the parameter subproblem of the ADMM-Inspired Momentum framework, AIMuon uses the gradient--momentum residual to correct the tentative spectral step. The residual undergoes a separate matrix-sign transformation, while spectral--nuclear duality determines the relative weighting of the momentum and residual directions. In practice, both directions are approximated with Newton--Schulz iterations and their combination is rescaled to match Muon's update magnitude. We establish a stochastic stationarity bound for the corresponding exact iteration. On GPT-2-small, GPT-2-medium, and Qwen3-0.6B, AIMuon reaches Muon's final validation loss with 8.98\%, 10.05\%, and 6.49\% fewer optimization steps, respectively, while achieving lower final validation loss than Muon, Muon-Nesterov, and MONA.

Machine Learning.title: Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Knowledge distillation improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by compressing the knowledge of a teacher LLM to train smaller LLMs. On-policy distillation advances this approach by having the student sample its own trajectories while a teacher LLM provides dense token-level supervision, addressing the distribution mismatch between training and inference in off-policy distillation methods. However, on-policy distillation typically requires a separate, often larger, teacher LLM and does not explicitly leverage ground-truth solutions available in reasoning datasets. Inspired by the intuition that a sufficiently capable LLM can rationalize external privileged reasoning traces and teach its weaker self, we introduce On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), a learning algorithm where a single LLM acts as both teacher and student with different contexts. The teacher policy conditions on privileged information (e.g., verified reasoning traces) while the student policy sees only the question; training minimizes the per-token divergence between these distributions over the student's own rollouts. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving superior token efficiency compared to reinforcement learning methods and better performance over off-policy distillation methods. Code repo: https://github.com/siyan-zhao/OPSD.

Machine Learning.title: Online Learning for Minimizing Maximum Tardiness in Single-Machine Scheduling
Machine Learning.summary:
We study online learning for minimizing maximum tardiness (\OMMT) in single-machine scheduling. In each round, the learner selects a permutation of \(n\) fixed jobs, representing a schedule. The environment then reveals a processing time and a due date for each job, and the learner incurs a vector-valued loss whose components correspond to the tardiness of the individual jobs. The goal of the learner is to minimize \(α\)-regret, the difference between the learner's maximum cumulative tardiness and \(α\) times that of the best fixed permutation in hindsight, for as small \(α\) as possible. We investigate OMMT under both stochastic and adversarial environments. In the stochastic setting, we prove that the expected \(1\)-regret of the Follow-the-Leader (FTL) algorithm is \(
  O\!\left(\frac{n\log n}{Δ^2}\right) \), together with a corresponding high-probability bound, where \(Δ\) is a distribution-dependent gap parameter. At round \(t \in \{1,\dots,T\}\), FTL runs in \(O(tn^2)\) time and \(O(tn)\) space. In the adversarial setting, we prove that, for any \(0<c<\log_2 n/16\), the \(α\)-regret is \(Ω(T)\) whenever \(α<\log_2 n/16-c\). We then reduce OMMT to a surrogate online learning problem and apply Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL), obtaining an expected \(α\)-regret bound of \(O(n^2\sqrt{T})\) for \(α=O(\log n)\). Thus, the logarithmic dependence of \(α\) on \(n\) is tight up to constant factors. Each FTPL update admits a mixed-integer programming formulation whose size is polynomial in \(n\) and \(t\).
Machine Learning.comment: Appears in the Proceedings of the 52nd International Conference on Current Trends in Theory and Practice of Computer Science (Sofsem 2027)

Machine Learning.title: COMPASS: Cross-modal Observation with Multi-Path Adaptive Stopping and Selection for Early Time Series Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Early time-series classification (ETSC) balances predictive performance against the amount of observed data. In multimodal settings, modality-associated and fused branches may differ in predictive ability at the same observed prefix, motivating joint decisions about when to stop and which branch should provide the final prediction. We propose COMPASS, a two-stage framework that preserves two modality-associated temporal branches and one fusion branch. The first stage combines cross-modal feature exchange and gated fusion with branch-wise supervision at every prefix. The second stage optimizes a shared four-action controller to continue observation or terminate through one of the frozen branches. Experiments on six physiological and wearable datasets compare COMPASS with multimodal adaptations of five ETSC baselines. COMPASS achieves the best average ranks in accuracy-earliness harmonic mean, AUROC, and earliness within this comparison set. At identical learned stopping times, branch selection improves mean accuracy over fusion readout on five of the six datasets, with gains of 2.35 and 2.16 percentage points on ISRUC-Sleep and UCDDB, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on joint stopping and branch selection for multimodal early time series classification.

Machine Learning.title: Rethinking Cross-Sensor Domain Adaptation for Bridge Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation
Machine Learning.summary: Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data. This study re-examines the SemanticBridge TLS-to-MLS protocol to determine how sampling density, surface roughness, color, and acquisition viewpoint are expressed in the 8-cm sparse-voxel representation, and how adaptation gains depend on source-model convergence. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net, we combine raw-point statistics with controlled input perturbations and compare adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, Mean Teacher, and confidence-filtered self-training under 100- and 300-epoch schedules. TLS and MLS have similar nearest-neighbor spacing after preprocessing (12.08 and 12.02 mm), and a 4-mm perturbation of TLS points changes voxel occupancy by only 4.4%. Color distributions differ systematically, but zeroing color on identical voxels changes target mean intersection over union (mIoU) by only +0.02, and by +0.06 after the color augmentation is scale-corrected. The sensors also observe different portions of the bridge, yielding different class proportions. A 300-epoch source-only model obtains 57.80 mIoU on the paired-bridge protocol. Confidence-filtered self-training improves the 100-epoch baseline, but from a converged model it changes target mIoU by -0.97 (source-selected checkpoints) and -2.44 (final-50-epoch means). Repeated evaluation (standard deviation 0.27-0.64) and seed variation (1.88 across three seeds) are comparable to several method differences. Adaptation results on this benchmark therefore depend on representation scale, source-model convergence, and evaluation variability.

Machine Learning.title: Structural Agreement Indicates Prediction Accuracy For Protein-Ligand Co-Folding
Machine Learning.summary: Co-folding models predict the structures of proteins and their bound ligands, but their accuracy varies across targets. Their usefulness therefore depends on knowing which predictions a user can trust. Confidence scores are intended to guide that choice. However, across seven co-folding models, we show that confidence-based selection offers little improvement over choosing a prediction at random. For approximately three-quarters of structures, predictions are either exclusively correct or incorrect, leaving no opportunity for ranking to change the outcome. Moreover, high confidence does not reliably discriminate correct top-ranked predictions from incorrect ones. We find that structural agreement among predictions is a more accurate measure of likely success than current confidence scores. We capture this with the Concentration of Repeated Ensembles (CORE) Score, which combines cluster tightness with ensemble support. CORE Score discriminates top-1 success and oracle success, achieving mean ROC AUCs of 0.866 and 0.838, compared to 0.757 and 0.759 for ipTM. CORE Score also outperforms training set similarity measures, including ligand Tanimoto, protein sequence, and Runs N' Poses similarity, despite requiring no experimental ligand pose. Structural agreement is therefore a practical indicator of reliability and a baseline for evaluating future confidence estimators, without requiring an additional trained uncertainty estimator.
Machine Learning.comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, 20 supplementary figures, 3 supplementary tables. Code: https://github.com/oxpig/core-score

Machine Learning.title: Fractal basin geometry and the limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning
Machine Learning.summary: Fundamental limits to predictability are central to our understanding of many physical and computational systems. In deep learning, training outcomes are often difficult to predict and reproduce even when extrinsic sources of randomness are controlled, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here we propose riddled basin geometry as a unifying dynamical systems mechanism: every initialization leading to one solution lies arbitrarily close to initializations leading to different solutions, forming a fat fractal with structure at arbitrarily fine scales. Using a minimal neural network model, we analytically establish the classical route to riddling and derive a near-zero uncertainty exponent: even sharp increases in initialization precision yield only marginal gains in outcome predictability. In deep networks, intertwined training destinations and near-zero parameter-space exponents provide robust signatures consistent with riddling across the tested architectures, optimizers and training protocols, offering a common dynamical account of otherwise disparate empirical observations. We further introduce functional uncertainty exponents, extending these diagnostics of scale-insensitive irreproducibility from parameter space to the learned functions themselves. Together, our results support riddled basin geometry as a candidate organizing principle for irreproducibility in deep learning, with practical implications for optimization and the reliable deployment of artificial intelligence.

Machine Learning.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
Machine Learning.summary: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

Machine Learning.title: Deep Learning-based Approaches for State Space Models: A Selective Review
Machine Learning.summary: State-space models (SSMs) offer a powerful framework for dynamical system analysis, wherein the temporal dynamics of the system are assumed to be captured through the evolution of the latent states, which govern the values of the observations. This paper provides a selective review of recent advancements in deep neural network-based approaches for SSMs, and presents a unified perspective for discrete-time deep state space models and continuous-time ones such as latent neural Ordinary Differential and Stochastic Differential Equations. It starts with an overview of the classical maximum likelihood based approach for learning SSMs, reviews the variational autoencoder as a general learning pipeline for neural network-based approaches in the presence of latent variables, and discusses in detail representative deep learning models that fall under the SSM framework. Very recent developments, where SSMs are used as standalone architectural modules for improving efficiency in sequence modeling, are also examined. Finally, we present examples involving nowcasting and irregularly sampled time-series data, together with a brief overview of scientific applications based on mechanistically structured SSMs.

Machine Learning.title: Action-Conditioned Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary: We study spatio-temporal forecasting in networked systems under specified actions. The challenge is to capture the action's effects without predicting spurious changes in unaffected regions. However, direct supervision and evaluation of these effects require paired futures with and without the action, whereas observational trajectories reveal only the realized future. We introduce PairST, a benchmark comprising six datasets across traffic, power transmission and water distribution, with paired reference and intervened futures simulated from the same system state. These pairs enable separate evaluation of affected-region forecast accuracy and quiet-region response error. We further propose ActionST, which forecasts the intervened future by writing an explicit response onto an intervention-independent reference forecast. Specifically, node-time addressing constructs a query for each response position, a state-conditioned response writer computes candidate responses, and a graph-aware locality gate controls their strength. Experiments on six datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ActionST at new action targets, with the lowest mean absolute error on five datasets and the best average rank. Our source code and the PairST benchmark are available at https://github.com/yutong-xia/ActionST.

Machine Learning.title: Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
Machine Learning.summary: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.

Machine Learning.title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.

Machine Learning.title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model
Machine Learning.summary: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.

Machine Learning.title: Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling in Federated Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Scheduling clients for model training is critical in federated learning due to both data and system heterogeneity. Most previous works focus on the quality of the scheduled clients to achieve faster convergence, shorter wall-clock convergence time, or better average model performance. They rarely consider the diversity of clients, which is important to counter heterogeneity and improve performance for the worst-off clients. In this work, we advocate the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) to model and enhance the diversity in client scheduling. We first design the kernel matrices of DPPs using gradient information and quality scores, which inherently enables a flexible quality-diversity trade-off. Applying fast MAP inference over DPPs, we propose Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling (ADCS) in FL. We further quantify the gradient approximation error of ADCS and develop convergence analysis for general biased client selection in FL with non-convex loss functions. We conduct comparative numerical experiments showing that ADCS outperforms state-of-the-art client scheduling algorithms, including both quality-based and diversity-based ones.

Machine Learning.title: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima
Machine Learning.summary: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.

Machine Learning.title: Towards Understanding On-Policy Distillation through the Lens of Test-Time Scaling
Machine Learning.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising post-training technique for enhancing LLM reasoning. Under the reverse KL objective, the idealized optimum of OPD aligns the student distribution with that of the teacher. When the teacher consistently outperforms the student, this naturally suggests that OPD should yield broad improvements over the pre-OPD student. However, do such improvements extend across the entire range of test-time sampling budgets? In this work, we revisit this expectation through the lens of test-time scaling by varying the sampling budget $K$ and evaluating performance with pass@$K$. Across multiple settings, we observe two distinct patterns: OPD can improve pass@$K$ at both small and large sampling budgets, but it can also improve small-budget performance while reducing large-budget pass@$K$. We show one condition that guarantees such a reversal and an idealized reverse KL counterexample where it occurs even when the teacher has higher accuracy on every problem. To choose between two candidate teachers at a target sampling budget, we propose the \textit{Teacher Advantage Score at $K$} (TAS@$K$), which can be computed before OPD training to predict which teacher will lead to a larger improvement in pass@$K$. Across three domains and thirteen benchmarks, the ordering predicted by TAS@$K$ agrees with the observed pass@$K$ improvements of the resulting OPD models in 83.6\% of experiments, providing a useful signal for teacher selection at the target pass@$K$.

Machine Learning.title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations
Machine Learning.summary: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. We introduce Ruby, a Robust Universal Binding affinitY predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model Pearl without requiring an explicit binding pose for every compound. Ruby is trained on proprietary data plus GenesisPotency-2026, an audited public-source potency training dataset released for academic and commercial use under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license with row-level provenance and audit annotations. Ruby achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment across seven public hit-identification targets among evaluated methods, with adjustable inference effort trading off enrichment and computational cost over more than two orders of magnitude. Ruby achieves the highest average correlations across four public benchmarks: OpenFE, CASP16, FEP+ 4, and OpenBind. Ruby significantly outperforms other methods in zero-shot prediction across eight biochemical and cellular assays from five ongoing Genesis-Incyte programs, widening its performance advantage relative to the public benchmarks. Ruby continues to improve more than other methods when all are given the opportunity to recalibrate using earlier assay measurements. Together, these contributions provide an annotated training resource for the field and a state-of-the-art potency predictor for broad screening, prioritization within related chemical series, and assay-specific prediction as experimental measurements accumulate.

Machine Learning.title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
Machine Learning.summary: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.

Machine Learning.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts
Machine Learning.summary: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source--target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

Machine Learning.title: Fair Property Tax: Reducing Regressivity in Machine-Learning Valuation
Machine Learning.summary: Advanced machine-learning models are increasingly used for property valuation in tax assessment. Although these models can achieve high predictive accuracy, they may systematically assign higher valuation-to-sale ratios to lower-priced properties, a pattern known as regressivity. In collaboration with the Cook County Assessor's Office (CCAO), we develop and evaluate two training methods that substantially reduce this regressive pattern while maintaining price-scale predictive accuracy. The Direct method has been incorporated into CCAO's public residential valuation software. Retaining the LightGBM model class used at CCAO, we propose a Direct penalty on squared covariance between log valuation errors and log sale prices, and an observation-additive Surrogate that yields a weighted squared-error loss. We evaluate both methods in our implementation of the CCAO workflow, using seven chronological validation folds, a held-out test set, and a 2025-forward test set. Measured by the magnitude of price-related bias (PRB), regressivity falls by approximately 49% on held-out sales and 39% on 2025 sales at a Surrogate setting selected by cross-validation, relative to the same LightGBM model fitted without the penalty. Price-scale $R^2$ is essentially unchanged. Its small rise, from 0.893 to 0.897 on held-out sales and from 0.904 to 0.908 on 2025 sales, reflects overall valuation level. Log-price RMSE rises by 3.1% and 1.7%, respectively. Paired sale-bootstrap 90% intervals for the PRB reductions lie within about two percentage points of these estimates. In an additional eight-county benchmark, both methods reduce regressivity in every county, with higher log-price prediction error as the expected tradeoff. These findings demonstrate a practical way to reduce measured regressivity within an existing assessor workflow while preserving price-scale predictive performance.

Machine Learning.title: RefDecoder: Enhancing Visual Generation with Conditional Video Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Video generation powers a vast array of downstream applications. However, while the de facto standard, i.e., latent diffusion models, typically employ heavily conditioned denoising networks, their decoders often remain unconditional. We observe that this architectural asymmetry leads to significant loss of detail and inconsistency relative to the input image. To address this, we argue that the decoder requires equal conditioning to preserve structural integrity. We introduce RefDecoder, a reference-conditioned video VAE decoder by injecting high-fidelity reference image signal directly into the decoding process via reference attention. Specifically, a lightweight image encoder maps the reference frame into the detail-rich high-dimensional tokens, which are co-processed with the denoised video latent tokens at each decoder up-sampling stage. We demonstrate consistent improvements across several distinct decoder backbones (e.g., Wan 2.1 and VideoVAE+), achieving up to +2.1 dB PSNR over the unconditional baselines on the Inter4K, WebVid, and Large Motion reconstruction benchmarks. Notably, RefDecoder can be directly swapped into existing video generation systems without additional fine-tuning, and we report across-the-board improvements in subject consistency, background consistency, and overall quality scores on the VBench I2V benchmark. Beyond I2V, RefDecoder generalizes well to a wide range of visual generation tasks such as style transfer and video editing refinement.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, update camera-ready version

Machine Learning.title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
Machine Learning.summary: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.

Machine Learning.title: NucleoNet: A Nuclear-Aware Determinant Ansatz for Multi-Geometry Neural Variational Monte Carlo
Machine Learning.summary: Neural-network variational Monte Carlo provides an accurate route to solving the electronic Schrödinger equation, but many neural wavefunctions are optimized for a single nuclear geometry, requiring separate calculations to map out a potential energy surface. We introduce NucleoNet, a nuclear-aware determinant ansatz that jointly evolves electronic and nuclear representations through a shared backbone, with antisymmetry enforced by electronic determinants. Across eight equilibrium small-molecule benchmarks, NucleoNet achieves energies comparable to established neural-wavefunction baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, totaling 0.10--0.13 million. For each molecular system, a single model optimized jointly across geometries describes the N$_2$ dissociation curve, Li displacement in LiCN, and the ethane and formamide minimum-energy paths for bond dissociation. Models trained on sparse geometry sets generalize to unseen configurations in N$_2$ and LiCN without further optimization. For N$_2$, training on six geometries yields a mean absolute error (MAE) of $1.13\ \mathrm{m}E_h$ on a 32-point evaluation grid, compared with $1.07\ \mathrm{m}E_h$ when optimized on all 32 geometries. Ablation studies on N$_2$ show that propagating nuclear representations improves geometric generalization under both shared and nucleus-specific envelope parameterizations.

Machine Learning.title: Distributional Algebro-Geometric Persistence (dAGP): Wasserstein-Stable Polynomial-Relation Signatures
Machine Learning.summary: A circle and a quartic superellipse have the same homology, but their defining equations have degrees two and four, respectively. We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $μ$ on $Ω=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $φ_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(μ)=\mathbb{E}_{X\simμ}[φ_m(X)φ_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(μ)c=\mathbb{E}_μ[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $μ$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $μ\mapsto G_m(μ)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range. A $100$-repetition sensitivity study quantifies onset recovery and shows that the count grid and two continuous spectral baselines nearly saturate the four-family discrimination task.
Machine Learning.comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Geometric Distributional Deep Learning (GDDL)

Machine Learning.title: Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale
Machine Learning.summary: AI coding agents (e.g., GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex) interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload different from chatbots. We present the first production-scale characterization of coding agents using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June-July 2026, comprising 7.4M users, 819M conversations, 5.7B LLM calls, and 946T tokens. Our analysis reveals distinctive workload properties with unique systems implications: e.g., sparse user-initiated turns unfold into autonomous agent loops with nearly 1:1 coupling between LLM calls and tool execution; parallel LLM calls are rare but exist in turns that trigger subagents; KV cache hit rates average 90% within a turn, but fall to 52% across turn boundaries and to 6% after model switches; workflows and user behaviors exhibit diverse, long-tailed resource footprints. We further distinguish short agentic turnaround times from minutes-long user idle periods between turns, and develop a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 87-89% of total idle time. We demonstrate two use cases: (1) a harness-side LLM API keep-alive policy that preserves provider-side context KV cache, reducing token costs by 14.9% on turn boundaries; and (2) a serving-side KV cache residency policy that uses predicted idle time to guide DRAM offloading, reducing time to first token (TTFT) by 3-33% compared with LRU during a one-week evaluation with GitHub Copilot traces.

Machine Learning.title: Affine-Image Propagation for Tight and Scalable Neural Network Verification
Machine Learning.summary: While bound propagation methods are highly effective for certifying neural networks against $\ell_{\infty}$ adversaries, tight and scalable verification for $\ell_{2}$ adversaries remains a significant open challenge. Existing methods incur geometric loss by enclosing preactivation sets in elementwise intervals or axis-aligned ellipsoids, and functional loss by restricting the linear bounds constructed over those domains. Consequently, tight $\ell_{2}$ verification is currently restricted to Lipschitz-regularized networks where these approximations are accurate. In this paper, we introduce affine-image SDP-CROWN, a novel bound propagation method that better approximates preactivation domains using affine-image constraints and jointly optimizes the linear bound to adapt to the resulting domain. To bypass the prohibitive computational cost of dense semidefinite constraints required by the affine-image representation, we replace them with scaled diagonal-dominance conditions, allowing a GPU-accelerated implementation. Our method preserves the bound propagation recursion and can be integrated with branch-and-bound. On five MNIST and CIFAR-10 non-Lipschitz-regularized networks, our method improves verified accuracy over state-of-the-art methods by 17% to 57.5%. With branch-and-bound, these improvements increase to between 27% and 63.5%.

Machine Learning.title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

Machine Learning.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria
Machine Learning.summary: The identification theory for causal effects in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with hidden variables is well established, but methods for estimation and inference beyond the g-formula remain less developed. Previous studies have introduced influence-function-based estimators for broad classes of identifiable effects. When implemented through the observed-data density factorization, these estimators can require conditional density estimation and numerical integration, which can be statistically challenging and computationally demanding for continuous or multivariate variables. Prior work on related causal functionals has used sequential regressions and Bayes-rule representations of density ratios to avoid these requirements. Building on established identification and influence-function results, we make these reparameterizations explicit for effects identified under treatment primal fixability, Tian and Pearl's necessary and sufficient condition for identification of post-intervention law, encompassing settings beyond classical back-door and front-door identification. We construct one-step estimators under alternative nuisance parameterizations and characterize how these choices affect robustness properties and nuisance-specific L2(P) product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and root-n consistency. The estimators accommodate data-adaptive machine learning for nuisance estimation. To address potential violations of the target parameter bounds by one-step estimators, we also develop targeted minimum loss-based estimators (TMLEs) that respect these bounds. Our robustness characterizations and sufficient rate conditions apply to both the one-step estimators and TMLEs. Building on prior efficiency theory for hidden-variable DAGs, we further develop modifications of our estimators that exploit ordinary independence restrictions. Implementations are provided in the R flexCausal package.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Arrow: From Impossibility to Possibility in Multi-Criteria Benchmarking
Machine Learning.summary: Modern benchmarks such as HELM MMLU account for multiple metrics like accuracy, robustness and efficiency. When trying to turn these metrics into a single ranking, natural aggregation procedures can produce cyclic pairwise comparisons or rankings that are unstable to changes in the model set. We formalize this aggregation as a social choice problem where each metric induces a preference ranking over models on each dataset, and a benchmark operator aggregates these votes across metrics. While prior work has focused on Arrow's impossibility result, we identify sufficient conditions under which the impossibility disappears and meaningful multi-criteria benchmarking becomes possible. In particular, we deal with three restrictions on the combinations of rankings and show that on single-peaked, group-separable and distance-restricted preferences, the benchmark operator allows for the construction of well-behaved rankings of the involved models. Empirically, we investigate several modern benchmark suites like HELM MMLU and verify which structural conditions are fulfilled on which benchmark problems.

Machine Learning.title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
Machine Learning.summary: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix.
